cards.truth: An object that caused a death – a cart, a boiler – forfeited to the crown as if the thing itself were guilty.
Funding a stranger's lawsuit in return for a cut of the winnings – once a crime, now basically an industry.
When someone dies with no will and no heirs, their property slides quietly back to the crown.
An officially accepted excuse for not turning up to court – the medieval sick note.
A medieval court on tour – royal judges riding from county to county to hear cases.
A half share of something – a word lawyers and chemists refuse to let go of.
Literally 'dead hand' – land held forever by a church or corporation that can never die.
A lawsuit for getting your own belongings back from someone who wrongly seized them.
The old Germanic price list for a killing – pay the family in silver, or face the feud.
The penalty that wiped out a traitor's legal existence – no rights, no property, nothing to inherit.
An old Kentish custom where a dead man's land was split equally between all his sons.
A medieval buddy system – ten households legally answerable for each other's behaviour.
The offence of stirring up quarrels and lawsuits for the sheer joy of it.
Seizing a debtor's belongings and holding them hostage until the bill gets paid.
A medieval fine set entirely at the court's mercy – hence the name.
Holding farmland by paying rent or doing chores for the lord – no fighting required.
The right to use and enjoy someone else's property, so long as you hand it back undamaged.
Being placed outside the law's protection entirely – harming an outlaw was no crime.
A medieval officer who hunted down debtors – the name literally means 'chicken chaser'.
A medieval tenant farmer bound to his lord's land – not enslaved, but not free to leave.
The earthy smell that rises when rain hits dry ground.
The medical name for goosebumps.
The housing that holds a ship's compass, standing right in front of the wheel.
A petty lie – or pretentious nonsense.
The soft, fading light just after sunset.
Fluffy sausages of frayed rope hung in the rigging so the sails don't chafe.
One of the curved timbers that form the ribs of a wooden ship.
The lowest deck of a ship, down where daylight gives up.
The block of soft sandstone sailors knelt with to scrub the deck – hence the pious name.
A small storage locker tucked into the stern of a boat.
The opening in the bow that the anchor cable runs through.
A stout beam jutting from the bow, used to hoist the anchor clear of the hull.
The socket a boat's rudder pivots in. Also, unhelpfully, a small fish.
The little peg on a boat's rail that a rowing oar pivots against.
The sliding collar that holds a ship's yard against the mast.
A polished wooden cone used to pry rope strands apart for splicing.
The rail running around the very back end of a ship.
Originally the ship's drinking-water cask – sailors gossiped around it, so the word came to mean gossip.
The front edge of a sail – or steering so close to the wind that it starts flapping.
The pointed metal spike sailors use to loosen stubborn knots and work rope.
An old English coin worth four pence.
A small beer cask – exactly a quarter of a barrel.
A beer cask holding half a barrel – two firkins, if you're keeping score.
Besides a moral qualm: a tiny apothecary weight of twenty grains.
An old unit for measuring cloth – the English ell ran to forty-five inches.
The formal medical term for sneezing.
The full-body stretch-and-yawn combination you perform on waking.
The small plastic or metal tip on the end of a shoelace.
A printing house's annual staff outing, traditionally held at the end of summer.
Scots for weather that is grey, damp and thoroughly joyless.
A narrow passage squeezed between buildings, in the north of England.
A Yorkshire word for a narrow shortcut alley.
A quiet country lane, in Cumbrian dialect.
A narrow wooded ravine with a stream tumbling through it.
A small stream, in northern English dialect.
The cold sea fog that creeps in off the North Sea and swallows whole towns.
Scots for rain so fine it seems to drift rather than fall.
Weather stuck halfway between mist and drizzle.
Sticky with mud – a clarty lane is the end of good shoes.
Unusually bothered by cold – the nesh one wants the heating on in September.
Sulky and moody, in the English Midlands – home of the mardy teenager.
To pester and fuss at someone until they finally crack.
The gap at the bottom of a hedge worn smooth by the regular passage of small animals.
The latch on a door or gate, in northern dialect.
Condition or working order – as in being in fine fettle.
Scots and Irish for the armpit.
Scots for vacant, daft and not quite switched on.
Scots for utterly soaked through – what a Bergen bus stop does to you.
Scots for pale, washed-out and in urgent need of sunshine.
A noisy uproar or scuffle – Scottish football commentary at its finest.
A hopeless tangle – the natural resting state of headphone cables.
The wooden rod Scots stir porridge with – it has its own world championship.
Scots for flashy and over-fancy – a fantoosh hat will get commented on.
A person who stands about idly watching canal boats go by.
American dialect for crooked, askew and generally out of line.
Three heavenly bodies in a straight line – like sun, moon and Earth during an eclipse.
The figure-eight the sun draws if you photograph it at the same time every day for a year.
Anticlockwise – against the sun's direction, which old folk considered bad luck.
The official name of the hash symbol on your keyboard.
The string of symbols that stands in for swearing in comic strips.
The little metal band that clamps the eraser to a pencil.
The slot a saw blade cuts – the wood that leaves as sawdust.
The curly metal shavings left behind by drilling and machining.
A reptile's version of hibernation – cold, sluggish and off its food.
To sleep away the summer, as snails do in a heatwave.
The medical term for a limb falling asleep.
The small groove running from your nose down to your upper lip.
The pale half-moon at the base of a fingernail.
The dot over a lowercase i or j.
Besides a kick and a flat boat: the dent pushed up into the bottom of a wine bottle.
A holder for a hot coffee cup – the cardboard sleeve counts as one.
A queasy stomach, or a proper case of the nerves.
To dawdle and fool around when you really should be getting on.
To pack up and clear off in a hurry, often with something that isn't yours.
American dialect for confusing someone completely.
A wobbly oatmeal pudding – which is why it also came to mean empty flattery.
An old English dessert of cream whipped up with wine and sugar.
Scots for a place to sit out in – a gazebo, or a quiet corner at a dance.
Relating to the day before yesterday.
The act of throwing someone – or something – out of a window.
